# Setting up OpenSpace and Web Server

# Setting Up OpenSpace and Web Server

Hello\! Welcome to this guide on how to set up the OpenSpace WWT replacement. This guide will assume that you have OpenSpace downloaded and placed in your C:\\ drive.

# 1 Getting the Files

## 1.1 Download the Files

To start off, let’s first download the required files from [Google Drive](https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/13fZRMRrnhMXLG0mIYn-XdwDi-id0djSg). Download the latest version by right-clicking on the folder and clicking “Download”. It’ll download the folder as a zip file.

![][image1]

When it is done downloading, extract the zip file and open the folder. Inside, you should see three folders: user-config, user-data-assets, and user-data-profiles. 

![][image2]

## 1.2 Move the Files

After downloading and extracting the folder, place the files in their correct place inside the OpenSpace folder. Open up another file explorer window and head to the OpenSpace folder. Then head to the \\users folder.

![][image3]

Head into the \\config folder. Go back to the downloaded folder window you had open previously and open up the \\user-config folder. Then select all the contents and move it to the OpenSpace \\config folder.

![][image4]

Now go back to the \\user folder and head into the \\data\\assets folder. In the other window, go back and open up the \\user-data-assets folder. Select all the contents and move it to the OpenSpace \\data\\assets folder. If you get a prompt asking if you want to replace files, I recommend making a copy of the \\assets folder somewhere before replacing the files.

![][image5]

Now for the final folder. Go back to the \\data folder and head into the \\profiles folder. In the other window, go back and open up the \\user-data-profiles folder. Select all the contents and move it to the OpenSpace \\data\\profiles folder.

![][image6]

# 2 Running OpenSpace and the Tablet Interface

## 2.1 Download Node.js

Once you’ve downloaded and placed the files in the correct directories, head to the \\user\\data\\assets\\WWT\\ web folder.

![][image7]

If you want to set up the web server to enable the tablet interface functionality, follow the following steps. Otherwise, you can just run start-all.bat and close the web server terminal. To install the web server, you must install Node.js. An executable MSI installer is provided to you in the \\web folder. You will need to have administrative privileges when installing. Click on node-v26.5.0-x64.msi and follow the steps shown on your screen. You may skip installing additional tools.

## 2.2 Running the Web Server

After you’ve finished installing, run start-web-server.bat to test if the web server works. It will install some libraries on the first run. You may get an administrator prompt. Click Allow, then restart your computer and run start-web-server.bat once again.

![][image8]

Once the libraries are installed, connect your web browser by going to the IP address shown in the terminal.

![][image9]

If you are able to access the website, great\! You can now also access the interface on a tablet by going to the IP address on a browser. Ensure that the tablet and the computer running the web server are connected to the same WiFi network. To then add the interface as a web app on an iOS tablet in Safari, go to the Share button in the top left corner. Click on “View More”, then click on “Add to Home Screen.”

## 2.3 Running OpenSpace

Once you’ve set up the web server and verified it working, you may now run OpenSpace. In the \\web folder, run start-all.bat which will run OpenSpace and the web server. Connect your tablet’s web browser to the web server. The website will occasionally reload until OpenSpace has finished initialization. Once OpenSpace has finished loading, you should be able to see the full interface on your tablet.

![][image10]  
/

The inside of the WWT folder should look like this:

base\_blank\_light\_WWT and base\_light\_WWT act as the bare bones of the program, only containing the Earth and Moon and setting up the GUI and default actions.

Below is a little schematic on what calls on what:

# Cache

## **1\. To Cache or Not to Cache**

Below are a list of locations that should be cached to optimize performance, please feel free to add to this list as more ground-based locations are added:

- Adler Planetarium  
- The Bean (Cloud Gate)  
- Tardigrade location on the Moon  
- Green Bank Telescope  
- Vera Rubin Observatory  
- Very Large Array  
- Mars poles  
- Valles Marineris

**Tardigrade Note:** When caching the location of the tardigrades on the Moon, it may appear as if they are in the ground and aren’t visible \- this is okay. After you are finished caching, simply restart OpenSpace and the tardigrades and lander should be visible.

**Crashing Issue:** Do not, under any circumstance, cache the Asteroid Belt. We attempted to cache the Asteroid Belt during testing to see if it loaded them up faster… it did not. In fact, it made the whole program crash and required the whole computer to be reset. So don’t do it. Please :)

# Telescopes

## **1\. Telescope Asset Management**

All asset files for both ground-based and space-based telescopes are located in WWT/scene/solarsystem/telescopes. Each telescope has its own subfolder and is loaded into OpenSpace via the master WWT\_telescopes asset file.

*![][image12]*

Several telescopes, including Green Bank, Hubble, JWST, and Spitzer, use default files already provided by OpenSpace or the OpenSpace Hub. We added the Vera Rubin Observatory ([model from NOIRLab](https://noirlab.edu/public/products/models3d/model3d005/)) and the Very Large Array ([model from NRAO](https://public.nrao.edu/gallery/vla-antenna-model/)) using a file structure that matches the default telescopes. 

**Hubble Space Telescope Note:** OpenSpace relies on Celestrak to load Hubble's orbital data. There has occasionally been a problem where, if the Celestrak website was down, OpenSpace would fail to launch entirely. The Hubble files were downloaded from the OpenSpace Hub and were made in 2024\. After communicating with OpenSpace developer Micah Acinapura, it has come to our attention that there is a new link for obtaining Hubble's orbital information ([https://liu-se.relay.openspaceproject.com/celestrak?CATNR=20580\&FORMAT=csv](https://liu-se.relay.openspaceproject.com/celestrak?CATNR=20580&FORMAT=csv)), and that the asset file needed an update in general. The Hubble file in the Final folder on the Google Drive is the most up-to-date file.

![][image13]

**Very Large Array (VLA) Details:** Each VLA antenna were placed manually. Their exact positions were plotted by locating the tracks for the D-configuration on Google Maps and pulling those coordinate points into the asset file. Additionally, the VLA .glb file contains a built-in animation, which could be an engaging feature to implement in the future. 

## **2\. Programming Ground-Based Telescope Actions** 

The action scripts that automate camera flights to the telescopes are found in WWT/actions/planets/telescope\_actions. 

![][image14]

Ground-based telescopes require a specific coding sequence so the camera doesn't accidentally clip through the Earth's surface.

1. **Set the idle motion:** Change the orbit type to `“OrbitAroundUpVector”`, in the code this is done by setting the IdleMotion type to ‘2’. This ensures the camera rotates around the telescope laterally without dipping below the terrain.  
2. **Fly to the location:** Use the `flyToGeo` command to navigate the camera to the telescope's exact geographic coordinates.  
3. **Snap the camera angle:** Use `scheduleScript` to apply a specific navigation state. This snaps the camera to a pre-defined, optimal viewing angle right after the flight finishes, ensuring the whole telescope is visible.  
4. **Activate idle motion:** Set a delay so the idle orbiting motion turns on only after the camera has arrived and positioned itself.

**How to capture the Navigation State for Step 3:**

* **Method 1 (Terminal):** 

  * Position your camera manually in OpenSpace. Press the \~ key to open the terminal and run: `openspace.printInfo(openspace.navigation.getNavigationState())`

![][image15] 

* Open your logs, set the filter in the top right to "Info", scroll to the bottom

![][image16]

* Copy the generated information into your code that should look something like this: *`openspace.scheduleScript([=[openspace.navigation.setNavigationState({Anchor = "Insert Anchor Here", Pitch = #, Position = { # , # , # }, Timestamp = "yyyy mmm dd hh:mm:ss", Up = { #, # , # }, Yaw = # }, false)]=], 15)`*

* **Method 2 (ShowComposer):**

  * Position your camera and open ShowComposer

![][image17] 

* Create a "Set Navigation Component" button and click "Set from Current Navigation State"

![][image18]

* Click your new button once to run it, open the Script Log, and copy the generated command into your asset file.

![][image19]

![][image20]

## **3\. Programming Space-Based Telescope Actions** 

Space-based telescopes like JWST and Hubble use a simpler sequence since groundclipping is not a concern.

1. **Focus first:** Command the camera to focus on the telescope *before* moving. This prevents aggressive, jarring camera snaps during the flight.  
2. **Fly to the target:** Use the standard `flyTo` command.  
3. **Reset orbit:** Explicitly set the orbital motion back to `“Orbit”` which is done by setting the IdleMotion type to ‘0’. This is necessary just in case the orbit type was previously changed by a ground-based script.  
4. **Activate idle motion:** Turn on idle motion so the camera begins orbiting the telescope immediately upon reaching its destination.

## **4\. Troubleshooting Camera Issues** 

* **Camera fails to snap into position for ground-based telescopes:** OpenSpace does not allow the camera to jump to a new navigation state while it is still actively flying. If the program lags, the flyTo action might take longer than your `scheduleScript` timer expects. Try increasing the timer delay in your script, or simply rerun the action in OpenSpace until the flight renders smoothly.  
* **Camera goes to the wrong place:** Some models handle reference frames differently. The VLA and Vera Rubin scripts specifically require the parameter `ReferenceFrame = Root` to work correctly. However, the Green Bank Telescope completely breaks if this is included. If you add a new model and it refuses to align correctly, try deleting the `ReferenceFrame` parameter entirely and setting the trailing boolean value to `false`.

# Adding Deep Sky Images

# Adding Deep Sky Images

## Amir Sabljic

Hello\! Welcome to this guide on how to add telescope images to our OpenSpace WWT replacement. This guide assumes that you know how to use OpenSpace and that you have [downloaded and placed the WWT replacement assets]() in their correct OpenSpace folder.

# 1 Finding and Downloading an Image

## 1.1 Find an Image

To start off, let’s first find an image. I’ll be going through an example in this guide of adding an image of the Triangulum Galaxy (M33). I highly recommend using one of ESA’s websites ([eso.org](http://eso.org), [esahubble.org](http://esahubble.org), [esawebb.org](http://esawebb.org), etc.) as they tend to give you all the information needed for the correct placement of the image in OpenSpace. The NOIRLab website ([noirlab.edu](http://noirlab.edu)) is also a good source for images from ground observations and provides the same placement information, however I often find it is not always accurate (we’ll talk more about how to correct image placement later). You may also use other websites as long as they give you the RA, Dec, and field of view or if you are willing to figure those out yourself.

Head to [eso.org/public/images](http://eso.org/public/images) and search up “triangulum”, the first image should lead you to [https://www.eso.org/public/images/eso1424a/](https://www.eso.org/public/images/eso1424a/). 

![][image21]

## 1.2 Download the Image

Before downloading, ensure that the image has the necessary information needed for placement. Additionally, check the credits and image usage policy before downloading. Scroll down until you see the Coordinates section. If the image does not have a Coordinates section, try finding another image. This information will be useful later on.

![][image22]

Once you’ve verified that, scroll back up to the Image Formats section. Right-click on any of the links that say “JPEG” and click “Save link as…”. I recommend going for the “Screensize JPEG” or “Publication JPEG” as the file size tends to be smaller.

![][image23]

Copy the image file name and save the image into the user\\data\\assets\\WWT\\scene\\telescopeimages\\ images folder.

![][image24]

# 2 Adding the Image to OpenSpace

## 2.1 The image\_data.csv File

Once you’ve downloaded the image and placed it in the correct folder, now we can go about adding it to OpenSpace. Head to the user\\data\\assets\\WWT\\scene\\telescopeimages\\images folder and open up image\_data.csv. You may open this up in Notepad, VSCode, Google Sheets, etc., just make sure the formatting does not change. For example in Google Sheets, make sure to turn off “convert text to numbers”.

![][image25]

After importing, select everything and go to Format \> Number and select “Plain text”.

![][image26]

The image\_data.csv is what is read by the telescope\_images.asset which then inserts all the listed images into OpenSpace. There are 9 columns in the csv file.

![][image27]

Here’s what each of the columns mean:

**group:** The object type (galaxies, nebulae, stars, etc.). This is also how the image actions/buttons are organized in OpenSpace and on the guest tablet (if using the web interface).  
**uniqueAbbrv:** The image’s identifier name in OpenSpace. This must be unique and cannot contain any illegal characters (no spaces, no punctuation marks, etc.).  
**name:** The image’s GUI name in OpenSpace. This name is what will be displayed on the guest-facing tablet, so make sure it’s simple and straightforward. If an object has both a scientific name and a more common name, I recommend listing the more common name first with the scientific name name in parentheses (e.g. The Crab Nebula (M1)).  
**ra:** The right ascension or longitude of the image, measuring the east-west angular position of an object on the celestial sphere.  
**dec:** The declination or latitude of the image, measuring an object's angular distance north (+) or south (-) of the celestial equator.  
**vertSize:** The vertical size of the image in arcminutes.  
**scale:** The scale of the image, for granular adjustments. Most of the time however this will be 1.0.   
**angleDeg:** The angle of the image relative to north in degrees. If north is 15 degrees to the right of the vertical edge, then it is \+15 degrees. If north is 15 degrees to the left of the vertical edge, then it is \-15 degrees.  
**imageName:** The exact file name of the image in the \\images folder.

## 2.2 Adding a New Line

Create a new line in the csv file. I recommend keeping the images grouped by type but this is not necessary. 

![][image28]

In this new line, start adding the necessary information from the image source website. Paste the image file name into the imageName column, and then add the type, unique abbreviation, and full name of the object.

![][image29]

Once you’ve done that, go back to the website where you’ve found the image and scroll down to the Coordinates section. Put in the Position (RA) and Position (Dec). For RA, the format is in 00h00m00.00s. For Dec, the format is \+/-00d00m00.00s. Ensure that you have it in this format.

![][image30]  
![][image31]

Now add the size of the image. This should be the vertical size (the second number, highlighted in blue below) that is shown in the field of view.

![][image32]  
![][image33]

For the scale, put 1.0. If the image size needs to be adjusted, change this value accordingly.

Now add the angle of the image. If north is to the RIGHT of the vertical, have the angle be positive (+). Likewise, if north is to the LEFT of the vertical, have the angle be negative (-).

![][image34]

In this example, north is 90 degrees to the left so I’ll put \-90 degrees in the column.

![][image35]

And there you have it\! Now head to OpenSpace to test it out.

# 3 Testing in OpenSpace and Making Adjustments

## 3.1 Testing in OpenSpace

To test and see if the image has been successfully added, you may either open OpenSpace using the WWT\_Replacement.profile or if you’d like to only load the telescope images, please download the [telescope-images-testing.profile](https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1nkcl-flfHJUssAUeQGDJizHeSgH7SpZZ?usp=drive_link) and use it instead. You may also want to download the earth\_axis.asset to help with orientation, otherwise disable it in the testing profile.

![][image36]

Once you’ve opened OpenSpace and launched it successfully, let’s go ahead to the image that we just added and see if it works. Head to the Actions on the OpenSpace dashboard.

![][image37]

Click on Deep Sky Objects, and then Galaxies.

![][image38]

Click on the image that you just created (In this case, the Triangulum Galaxy). Give it a moment to point to the image.

![][image39]

If you can see the image and no errors show up, you’re set\! Final check: Go to Scene and Pop out the image details at the top. Check if the image is correctly aligned by changing the opacity and looking at the stars in the background. If they seem to be in the same place then you’re done\!

![][image40]

## 3.2 Making Adjustments

If for some reason the image isn’t aligned correctly, you can attempt to get the correct RA and Dec using WorldWideTelescope or other browsers. Head to [https://worldwidetelescope.org/webclient/](https://worldwidetelescope.org/webclient/) and click on Search at the top. Search up the object and try to find the same image that you have. If you cannot find it, you may have to make minor adjustments yourself until it looks right.

![][image41]

After clicking on the image, look in the bottom right corner for the RA and Dec. Go back to the csv file and change the RA and Dec to the values from WWT. You can then reload the telescope\_image.asset using the Assets window in OpenSpace and check to see if the alignment is better.

![][image42]

# Constellations

## **1\. Constellation Asset Files**

The constellation system is divided into two primary asset files to separate the line-work from the artwork.

* **Lines and Labels:** The file responsible for toggling the basic constellation lines and their text labels is located at WWT/scene/digitaluniverse/constellations\_WWT.

![][image43]

* **Art and Actions:** The file that controls toggling the constellation illustrations, as well as the specific action scripts to trigger individual constellations, is found at WWT/scene/milkyway/constellations/constellation\_art\_WWT.

![][image44]

## **2\. Understanding Constellation Modes**

Because OpenSpace allows users to select different types of constellations, overlapping properties can cause visual bugs (e.g., the trails toggling back on when switching from looking at all constellations to only zodiacs).

To prevent these conflicts, the code relies on an `if/then` system checking two specific tracking variables: `constellationMode` and `constellationLineMode`. Both variables use the exact same logic to determine what should be displayed on screen:

* **Mode 0:** No constellations are currently visible.  
* **Mode 1:** All constellations (both zodiac and non-zodiac) are visible.  
* **Mode 2:** Only the zodiac constellations are visible.  
* **Mode 3:** An individual constellation is currently highlighted.

Whenever a user clicks a button, the script checks these mode numbers to decide what needs to be turned on or explicitly turned off.

![][image45]

## **3\. Visual Transitions & Scene Cleanup**

When turning on the constellations, the script performs a series of automated background actions to ensure the user has a clean, unobstructed view of the sky.

1. **Center the view:** The camera automatically anchors to the Sun to provide a centralized vantage point.  
2. **Reduce glare:** The Sun’s glare is turned off so it doesn't block out the constellations.  
3. **Clear the background:** All planetary orbital trails are faded down to remove visual clutter.  
4. **Hide planet labels:** You will notice a massive block of code dedicated to fading out planet labels. While planet labels are turned off by default, this code acts as a fail-safe. If a user was just looking at the "Entire Solar System" view (which turns labels on) and clicked directly to the constellations, the labels would normally stay stuck on the screen. This code forces them to hide.

## **4\. Automated Resets & The Ticket System**

To keep the exhibit moving, OpenSpace has been programmed to automatically reset the visual state after a certain number of seconds.

**Reset Action:** Once the timer finishes, the system triggers the `ClearConstellationFocus` action. This gracefully fades out the constellation art/lines and restores the Sun’s glare and orbital trails.

**Ticket Counter:** To prevent visual glitches when users rapidly click through different constellations, a ticket counting system was implemented. If a user clicks a second constellation while the first one is still visible, the ticket system intercepts the action and restarts the reset timer. This ensures the new constellation doesn't fade out prematurely based on the timer of the first click.

![][image46]

## **5\. Troubleshooting Camera Focus Issues**

* **Initial Individual Constellation Focusing:** You may encounter an issue where focusing on an individual constellation for the very first time brings up the correct art, but the camera points at completely the wrong patch of sky. This is suspected to be a coordinate system glitch. When OpenSpace tries to anchor the camera to the Solar System Barycenter for the very first time, the coordinate shift causes the camera to misalign. To solve this, a `scheduleScript` was added containing a `RetargetAim` command. This forces the camera to pause for 1 second after the button is pressed, and then explicitly refocus on the selected constellation. If this targeting bug occurs again in future updates, try increasing that 1-second delay timer before attempting other changes.

# Asteroids

## **1\. Asteroid Assets & 3D Models**

All asteroid models and data are loaded into OpenSpace via the primary asteroid file located at WWT/scene/solarsystem/asteroids/asteroids. Each asteroid group has its own subfolder and is loaded into OpenSpace via the master asteroids asset file.

![][image47]

Several files for asteroids, including the data for the Asteroid Belt (AB), Potentially Hazardous Asteroids (PHAs), and the asteroid/dwarf planet Vesta already existed in OpenSpace and simply needed to be loaded in. We added Oumuamua ([model from Ignazio Pillitteri on Sketchfab](https://sketchfab.com/3d-models/oumuamua-an-alien-visitor-b6da77110c92402f9e01d2654ddb2431)) and Psyche. Because it was difficult to find a high-quality, free 3D model of the asteroid Psyche, a model of the asteroid Bennu ([taken from the NASA 3D Resources page](https://science.nasa.gov/3d-resources/asteroid-101955-bennu/)) was used as a visual placeholder.

## **2\. Programming the Asteroid Belt (AB) & PHAs**

The action scripts that control toggling and flying to these asteroid groups are housed in WWT/actions/asteroids/asteroid\_actions.

![][image48]

The script to reveal the entire Asteroid Belt is one of the more complex sequences. Here is exactly what the code is doing step-by-step:

1. **Center the Solar System:** The camera is commanded to focus on the Sun. This ensures that the Solar System, and therefore the AB, is centered on the screen.  
2. **Zoom Out:** After a brief 0.1-second delay (to give OpenSpace time to lock onto the Sun), the camera automatically zooms out to a distance of roughly 2 light-hours (2,159,000,000,000 meters) so the entire belt fits on the screen.  
3. **Reset Orbit Type:** The orbit type is explicitly forced back to `"Orbit"`. Again, this is a safety measure in case the user flew to a ground-based telescope previously, which changes the camera mechanics.  
4. **Manage Visibility:** The script fades in the inner planet labels and adjusts their size. Because OpenSpace separates the Asteroid Belt into three distinct components (inner, main, and outer), the script must manually fade all three in. It also explicitly fades out the PHAs to prevent visual clutter.

The script for the Potentially Hazardous Asteroids (PHAs) follows a nearly identical camera setup, but shifts the main focus. Instead of all the inner planets, it only fades in the Earth label (making it slightly larger than it was in the AB labels). It then actively hides the other planet labels and the AB to isolate the PHAs.

## **3\. The "Double Idle Motion" Workaround**

You will notice a little quirk in the code for both the AB and PHAs that the command to turn on idle motion is written twice.

Normally, the script waits for the camera to finish zooming out (we set the delay to 10.5 seconds) before turning on idle motion. However, a bug was discovered that if the camera was already zoomed out to 2 light-hours when the user clicked the button, the camera would just sit perfectly still for 10.5 seconds doing nothing.

To fix this, a second idle motion command was added at the very top of the script with a tiny 0.5-second delay. If the camera is already in position, this early command catches it and starts orbiting immediately. If the camera isn't in position, the active zooming motion simply overrides the early command, and the 10.5-second command seamlessly takes over once the zoom finishes.

## **4\. The Dual Ticket System**

Like the constellations, the asteroids use a ticket timer system to reset the view after 30 seconds. However, the asteroids use a dual ticket system to solve a specific UI conflict where the Asteroid Belt timer wants to fade out all inner planet labels but the PHA timer wants to preserve the Earth label.

If a user rapidly clicks between the AB and the PHAs, the timers can get confused and accidentally fade the Earth label out at the wrong time. To prevent this, an overarching master `AsteroidCounter` tracks interactions between *both* systems. If the user clicks back and forth, this master counter overrides the individual `AsteroidBeltCounter` and `PHACounter` to ensure the Earth label stays perfectly visible.

![][image49]

![][image50]

## **5\. Individual Asteroid Flights & Rendering Fix**

The scripts to fly to individual objects (Oumuamua, Psyche, Vesta) are much simpler. The orbit type is set to "Orbit", the camera focuses on the asteroid, executes a 10-second flight, and applies idle motion upon arrival.

**Rendering Note (FaceCulling):** Because Oumuamua and Psyche use custom-imported 3D models rather than OpenSpace native assets, their geometry renders a bit strangely. To make their rocky skin textures look solid and correct, you must disable a setting called `FaceCulling` in their configurations. This step hasn’t been necessary for native assets like Vesta.

**Important Note on Vesta:** Since Vesta was a native asset to OpenSpace, we kept the file paths the same and left the model asset file for Vesta in the WWT/scene/solarsystem/dwarfplanets directory. However, in our research, we have found that Vesta is not officially a dwarf planet. This led us to include the action to fly to Vesta in the asteroids action folder.

![][image51]

![][image52]

# Tardigrades

## **1\. The Concept & Location**

Tardigrades are taking over the Moon\!\!\! They are anchored to the exact coordinates of the Beresheet lunar lander, which crashed in the Moon’s Sea of Serenity on April 11, 2019\.

This easter egg operates on a playful, hypothetical scenario: what if the Sea of Serenity was an actual sea like on Earth and contained liquid water? In this simulation, when the tardigrades crash-landed, they rehydrated and immediately began reproducing on the lunar surface.

## **2\. Managing Reproduction & System Performance**

Animating dozens of 3D models appearing over time is obviously going to be resource-intensive. The tardigrade code went through several iterations to balance the visual effect of reproduction against OpenSpace’s processing limits. If you need to tweak how the tardigrades behave, you can refer to these historical versions to understand what works and what causes crashes:

* **Version 1 (Basic):** Simply spawns two static tardigrade models that remain visible from April 2019 to April 2021\.  
* **Version 2 (Crash Hazard):** Programmed to be the most biologically accurate and randomize reproduction every time OpenSpace loads. It spawns 1 to 30 tardigrades every two weeks within a random 5-meter radius. **Warning:** This frequently pushed the model count past 600, overloading OpenSpace's renderer and causing the software to crash.  
* **Version 3 (Stacking Bug):** Attempted to fix the crashes by limiting the spawn rate to exactly 5 tardigrades every two weeks at a *constant* 5-meter distance. While it stopped the crashes, the models spawned perfectly stacked on top of the exact same 5 coordinates. It looked like reproduction had stopped entirely.  
* **Version 4 (Sweet Spot):** Fixed the stacking bug. It spawns 5 tardigrades every two weeks for two years, but scatters them randomly within a 5-meter radius. This creates a realistic spread without crashing the program.  
* **Version 5 (Quick Test):** Spawns 5 tardigrades every 5 seconds over the course of just one minute. This is the best version to use if you are actively testing code or wanting to record independent visuals, as it loads fast while still demonstrating the reproduction animation.

**Showcase Version:** The current live version triggers the first tardigrades to pop up on April 11, 2019 (the crash date). They reproduce at a rate of 5 tardigrades every 14 days for one year, and the colony remains populated until January 1, 2500\.

* **Important Note:** Because the exhibit is permanently locked to the fixed date of August 2, 2026, the reproduction animation has already finished by the time the user arrives. If you want to actually watch them reproduce, you will need to scrub the OpenSpace timeline backward to 2019\.

## **3\. Positioning & Terrain Troubleshooting**

* **Tardigrade Altitude:** Because the tardigrades are parented to the Beresheet lander rather than the Moon itself, their default "zero" height is the height that is the center of the lander's 3D model. To prevent the tardigrades from floating mid-air along the lander, their altitude is manually set to \-1.9. This negative value pushes them downward so they sit nicely on the lunar floor.

* **Height Map Glitches:** OpenSpace dynamically loads high-resolution height maps for the Moon's terrain, and this loading process can occasionally be inconsistent. Depending on how the terrain renders on a given day, you might find the tardigrades/lander hovering above the ground or buried completely underneath it. If the terrain shifts, simply wait for the map to finish loading and hope they pop back up, reload OpenSpace, or adjust the \-1.9 altitude setting up or down in small decimal increments until the tardigrades/lander sit flush with the surface again.

# Satellites

## **1\. Satellite Assets & Action Files**

Unlike the custom telescopes or tardigrades, the satellites are a default asset built directly into OpenSpace. Because of this, there is no special 3D model loading required. All of the custom work for this feature exists entirely within the action scripts, which dictate how the camera behaves when interacting with the satellites.

You can find the action scripts that handle toggling the satellites in WWT/actions/planets/satellites\_actions.

![][image53]

## **2\. Smart Camera & Toggle Logic**

When a user clicks a button to view a specific group of satellites, the script uses tracking variables (switching between `true` and `false`) to determine what to show. To ensure the user gets the best possible view, the script runs through a highly automated sequence:

1. **Check Earth Anchor:** The code first checks if the camera is currently anchored to Earth. If the user happens to be looking at Mars or the Sun, the script will automatically fly the camera back to Earth so the satellites are actually visible.

![][image54]

2. **Exclusive Visibility:** To clearly highlight a specific type of satellite, the script explicitly fades out all other satellite groups.  
3. **Smart Zooming:** The script uses the `zoomToDistance` command to snap the camera to the exact orbital altitude of the selected satellites. If the user clicks "All Satellites," the script calculates the distance of the satellites with the furthest orbit and zooms out to that maximum boundary.  
4. **Activate Idle Motion:** Once the camera reaches the appropriate zoom distance, idle motion is automatically enabled so the camera gracefully orbits the satellite swarm.

## **3\. Automated Resets & The Ticket System**

Just like the constellations and asteroids, the satellites utilize a ticket counter system to handle automated resets. When a user clicks a satellite toggle, it starts a 15-second countdown. If the user clicks another satellite button before time is up, the ticket counter resets the timer. This prevents the visuals from fading out prematurely while the user is still actively exploring.

* **Reset Note:** When the 15 seconds finally run out, the script calls upon a helper action named `ClearSatellites` to fade everything out and reset the view. By default, OpenSpace will automatically display the `ClearSatellites` action as a visible, clickable button in the Web Interface. Because this is just a background helper script, you don't really want/need guests clicking it. You will need to manually hide this action in the JavaScript file (refer to the *How to Change the Web Interface* section for instructions).

## **4\. Space Stations: ISS & Tiangong**

In addition to the satellite swarms, there are two specific actions dedicated to flying closely to the International Space Station (ISS) and the Tiangong space station.

Because these are individual objects rather than massive orbital groups, their scripts are much more straightforward. The sequence simply involves:

1. Making sure the camera's orbit type is set back to the default `"Orbit"`.  
2. Executing the flight to the space station.  
3. Applying idle motion the moment the camera stops flying so it smoothly circles the station.

# Adding Descriptions to the Web Interface

# Adding Descriptions to the Web Interface

## Amir Sabljic

Hello\! Welcome to this guide on how to add descriptions to the OS WWT web interface. This guide will assume that you have already [set up OpenSpace and the web server](). 

# 1 Adding Descriptions

## 1.1 The descriptions.json File

Head to the user\\data\\assets\\WWT\\web folder and open up descriptions.json in a text editor of your choice. The descriptions.json is what is read by the app.js which then displays the description based on what the camera is Aiming at in OpenSpace. It also holds translations for any UI elements (not done implementing).

![][image55]

The json is organized by categories. “ui” handles the ui elements, “folders” handles the folder names, “actions” handles the buttons, and “openspace” handles the descriptions of the object being displayed on OpenSpace.

## 1.2 Adding a New Description

To add a new description of an OpenSpace object, create a new line under “openspace” and follow the json format. Ensure that the name is the exact same name as the GUI name (not the identifier\!) in OpenSpace. Here I’ll go through an example of adding a description using Vanessa’s Beresheet Lander. First, find the object in OpenSpace or open up the asset file. Find the GUI name and copy it.

![][image56] ![][image57]

Once you’ve done that, write a new line under “openspace” and write the GUI name in quotes. Then add a semicolon. Add brackets and then write “en”. This will be the English description that is shown by default. For other translations, such as Spanish, you’ll put “es”. The translation functionality isn’t fully implemented yet.

![][image58]

Now put the description inside the quotes. Additionally, if you want to organize the json file to make it easier to navigate, you may do so. I’ll be putting the Beresheet inside of Missions after the Solar System.

![][image59]

Once you’re done, save the json file.

## 1.3 Testing in the Web Interface

If you already have the web interface up and running, you can just reload the website and the description should show when you focus on the object.

![][image60]  
/

# Modifying the Web Interface

# Modifying the Web Interface

## Amir Sabljic

Hello\! Welcome to this guide on how to modify certain characteristics of the OS WWT web interface. This guide will assume that you have already [set up OpenSpace and the web server](). 

# 1 Modifying the Web Interface

## 1.1 The config.js File

Some parts of the web interface can be modified without having to change the scripting in app.js. Head to the user\\data\\assets\\WWT\\web folder and open up config.js in a text editor of your choice. The config.js allows you to hide actions/buttons, hide folders/categories, and adjust the toggle timers of the buttons.

![][image61]

## 1.2 Hiding Certain Actions/Buttons

To hide certain actions/buttons, all you have to do is add the identifier of the action from OpenSpace into the BLOCKED\_ACTIONS array. To find the identifier of the action in OpenSpace, you can either look in the asset files of the specific action, or find it in OpenSpace by clicking on the ⓘ icon next to the action and copying, or by running the action and looking at the Script Log.

![][image62]  
![][image63]  
![][image64]

Once you’ve found the identifier of the action that you want to hide in the web interface, create a new line and put the identifier within quotation marks.

![][image65]

Save the js file and reload the web interface if you have it running. You should see the button has disappeared\!

![][image66] ![][image67]

## 1.3 Hiding Certain Categories/Folders

To hide certain folders/categories, you simply place the name of the folder inside the BLOCKED\_CATEGORIES array. If you want to hide the Missions folder for example, simply put ‘Missions’ in a new line inside the array.

![][image68]

Save the js file and reload the web interface if you have it running. You should see the folder is now gone.

![][image69] ![][image70]

## 1.4 Button Toggle Timers

When a user presses on a button, it’ll turn yellow to indicate that it has been pressed. The length of time that the button stays yellow can be modified depending on what folder the button is in. To do that, simply place the name of the folder inside the FOLDER\_TIMEOUTS dictionary. Ensure that the name is lowercase and remove all spaces. For example, if you wanted the buttons in the Missions folder to always be on until another button has been pressed, write a new line and put ‘missions’: null.

![][image71]

Save the js file and reload the web interface if you have it running. If you now click on Vostok 1 inside the Missions folder, you should see it stay yellow until you press another button.

![][image72]

# 2 Advanced Modifications

## 2.1 The app.js File

For more advanced modifications, the app.js is where all the web interface scripting is handled. This script loads all the actions from OpenSpace, organizes them into their categories, and creates the html for the interface. Additionally, the script also handles the info panel and object description on the right side of the screen. There is some code that handles text translations but it hasn’t been fully implemented.

## 2.2 The server.js File

The server.js is how the web interface talks to OpenSpace. This script handles connecting to the OpenSpace web socket and auto-reloading the web interface if OpenSpace disconnects. It also outputs any connections and disconnections to the terminal.  
/

# Known Issues and Ideas for the Web Interface

# Known Issues and Ideas for the Web Interface

This document contains a list of known issues with the web interface and also ideas for future implementation. This is intended to be a living document.

# Known Issues

## Toggle Sync

Because of the way actions work in OpenSpace, we weren’t able to implement a way for OpenSpace to communicate to the website if an action has been toggled on or off and to then reflect that change to the user. As a result, the toggles are handled by the website independently using timers for certain categories (ex: constellation toggle is highlighted yellow “on” for one minute and then turns blue “off”). When adding new actions in OpenSpace that have an idle period, ensure that it is also reflected in the website by adding an idle timer to the config.js file. A proper solution would probably be to use UserProperties and have every action have a custom property but this would require going through all the actions and modifying the code. See example code: 

openspace.addCustomProperty("StarSearchSelection","StringProperty","Selected Star", "Star selected from search",'openspace.setPropertyValueSingle("ScreenSpace.StarSearchDomePanel.Reload"')

openspace.setPropertyValueSingle("UserProperties.StarSearchSelection","Mizar")

openspace.printWarning(openspace.propertyValue("UserProperties.StarSearchSelection"))

## Folder Organization in the Web Interface

While you can organize the Scene GUI in OpenSpace, it doesn’t seem like you can organize the Actions GUI. If there is, I’m unsure if the order is then replicated to the web interface. A solution to this would probably be to have there be an order set in the config.js file that the app.js reads when importing the actions from OpenSpace, but I didn’t have enough time to implement this.

# FAQ’s

## **1\. Frequently Asked Questions & System Quirks**

When developing in OpenSpace, you might run into a few unique quirks. Here are the most common issues and how they are handled in this project, as well as smoke things that are just good to know (some of these things may have already been said in their individual sections but are just repeated here for simplicity):

**1.1 The Exhibit Time is Frozen**

To keep the exhibit consistent for every guest, the simulation time is permanently paused. The global time is fixed to **August 2, 2026, at 21:19:42 GMT**. If you are building new features like planetary alignments or satellite positions, or just want to give guests the option to time travel, remember that they will always render based on this specific date.

**1.2 Preventing Camera Clipping (The Orbit Rule)**

When writing camera actions, you have to manage two different styles of orbiting:

* **Ground-based objects:** You must set the orbit type to `"OrbitAroundUpVector"`. If you don't, the camera will treat the object like a planet in space and clip straight through the ground.  
* **Space-based objects:** Because ground-based scripts permanently change the camera's behavior, any script flying back out to a space-based object (like a planet or satellite) must explicitly reset the orbit type back to the default `"Orbit"`.

![][image73]

**1.3 Dealing with Unwanted UI Buttons**

OpenSpace will automatically generate a visible button in the Web Interface for every single action script you write. We often used helper actions (like the 15-second reset timers) that are only meant to be triggered by other code, not by guests. To clean up the menu, you must manually hide these helper actions in the JavaScript file. (Refer to the [*Modifying the Web Interface*]() section of the documentation for exact steps).

**1.4 Restoring Digital Universe Files**

All the asset files for the Digital Universe are safely stored in the WWT folder on the Google Drive. However, to keep the exhibit running smoothly, anything we didn’t specifically want to show was commented out inside the digitaluniverse\_WWT asset file. If you ever want to add those features back in, simply open that file and remove the comment tags.

![][image74]

**1.5 Asset Folder Quirks (Vesta)**

Be aware of a slight organizational quirk: the 3D model asset files for Vesta are located in the dwarf planets subfolder, but the action scripts that control flying to it are stored in the asteroids subfolder.

![][image75]  
![][image76]

**1.6 Hubble & Celestrak Startup Crashes**

As mentioned in the telescope section, we encountered an error with the Hubble asset files downloaded from the OpenSpace Hub. There has since been an update in how the orbital data is received by OpenSpace and the correct file is loaded on the drive. Should problems persist, reach out to the OpenSpace slack. We specifically spoke with OpenSpace developer Micah Acinapura.

**1.7 The Harmless Ceres Warning**

When you launch OpenSpace, you will likely get a flood of red warnings in the console stating that a scene graph node for "CeresPosition" and "Ceres" already exists and cannot be added. You can completely ignore this. The cause is unknown, but Ceres loads and functions perfectly fine regardless.

![][image77]

## **2\. Future Ideas & Guest Wishlist**

During development and guest testing, several great ideas came up that didn't make it into the current build. If you are to continue this project, these are fantastic places to start:

| Category | Idea | Implementation Notes |

| **3D Models** | The Adler Planetarium | Add a 3D model of the Adler Planetarium. |
|  | Beresheet Lander Skin | Find or create a proper high-resolution texture/skin for the Beresheet lander model. |
|  | Vostok 1 Bounding Sphere | Fix the bounding sphere for the Vostok 1 capsule model. Currently, when flying to Vostok, the camera gets super close before snapping back out. |
| **Guest Requests**  | Telescope Distance Panels  | Add more information to the description panels on the Web UI showing exactly how far space telescopes are from Earth. (Since the exhibit time is permanently fixed, this distance would be a constant number).  |

|  | Exoplanet/Star Systems | Add the ability to fly to or look at other star systems beyond our own.  |
